raptor: 12 capabilities, on both CPU and GPU, 11 on the Simulation side and 1 on the AI side.

Show details
  • Fixed-step ODEs CPU ✓ GPU ✓ A step written for one sample, run over the batch until every sample is done.
  • Differentiable sensitivities CPU ✓ GPU ✓ Every hawk kernel carries generated forward- and reverse-mode derivatives.
  • Zero-copy hand-over (DLPack) CPU ✓ GPU ✓ DLPack hand-over, certified with CuPy, PyTorch, NVIDIA Warp and NumPy.
  • Per-sample models and RHS CPU ✓ GPU ✓ You write one step of one sample; the batch is launched for you.
  • Ensembles and Monte Carlo CPU ✓ GPU ✓ Many independent samples in one batched run.
  • Divergent workloads CPU ✓ GPU ✓ Finished samples are compacted out, so each launch covers only the samples still running.
  • Events and early exit CPU ✓ GPU ✓ A sample stops on its own condition and leaves the work.
  • Adaptive ODEs, embedded pairs CPU ✓ GPU ✓ eagle.simulate runs an embedded RKF7(8) pair with per-sample step control.
  • Deployment outside Python CPU ✓ GPU ✓ A compiled kernel is embedded in a C++ program and run there.
  • Differentiable simulation into learning CPU ✓ GPU ✓ Gradients through a whole captured run.
  • Ensemble data for training CPU ✓ GPU ✓ Simulated batches feed a PyTorch training loop without copies.
  • Hybrid, physics-informed models CPU ✓ GPU ✓ A network and a physics model in one differentiable program.

What each tool has a documented, first-class way to do, on CPU and on GPU; speed is in the bars and the radar.

An icon lights up only when the tool's own documentation shows a designed feature or API for it; a workaround (masking every lane, raw CUDA strings, running the slowest sample to the end) does not count. Every covered cell links to its source. The tools are complementary; overlap is not a ranking.

Hover or focus an axis name (or a marker) to see what it measures, where its number comes from, and every tool's value on it.

  1. 1 Uneven ensembles faster is better
  2. 2 Regular ensembles faster is better
  3. 3 Small jobs faster is better
  4. 4 Adaptive ODEs faster is better
  5. 5 Memory smaller is better
  6. 6 Compile time lower is better
  7. 7 Code size smaller is better
  8. 8 Tensor workloads (qualitative)

  16. 16 Extensibility (qualitative)
Uneven ensembles
How long a batch takes when every sample stops at its own step, at the largest batch.
Regular ensembles
How long a batch takes when every sample runs the same number of steps, at the largest batch.
Small jobs
Wall time of the smallest batch, where launch overhead matters most.
Adaptive ODEs
Wall time of an adaptive-step orbit propagator (RK7(8)) at the largest batch.
Memory
Peak memory the process holds for the same workload (device memory on a GPU; host memory on a CPU at N = 1,000,000 only, net of the benchmark harness's own copies).
Compile time
Cold compile of the complex adaptive kernel (RK7(8) orbits) on empty caches; the simple oscillator's time and the growth factor are listed per tool. A tool with nothing to compile sits at the edge. Compiled once per kernel; raptor's compile does not depend on the problem size N.
Code size
Lines of code the task takes, non-blank and non-comment.
Tensor workloads (qualitative)
Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.
Array-style programming (qualitative)
Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author's judgement.
Half precision and below (qualitative)
Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author's judgement.
Single-thread abstraction (qualitative)
Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author's judgement.
Differentiable kernels (qualitative)
Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool's own vocabulary.
Low-level control (qualitative)
Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU's execution you control from the tool's own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author's judgement.
Works with your arrays (qualitative)
Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.
Deploy outside Python (qualitative)
Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.
Extensibility (qualitative)
Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author's judgement.

Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.

NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.

How to read this radar

Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.

  • Ensemble speed: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.
  • Footprint and turnaround: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.
  • Tensors and precision: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.
  • One-sample authoring: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.
  • Low-level control: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.
  • Reach: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.

Each measured axis is stretched over its own best-to-worst range, so ring labels differ per axis (compile time: fixed, 0.1 s to 100 s; code size: at least 4x). Axes are grouped by theme, so read the axes, not the area.

Italic axes are the author's judgement, not measurements: hollow markers, a linear scale, and no marker where a tool has no reading. A hollow marker on a measured axis means a minor is missing or, for compile time, is the tool's simple-kernel time. The hover panel has each axis's full wording.

  • Tensor workloads: 5 = dense array maths, batched linear algebra and convolutions are its home ground.
  • Array-style programming: 5 = the whole-array expression is the programming model.
  • Half precision and below: 5 = FP16, BF16, FP8, FP4 and tensor cores are first-class paths.
  • Single-thread abstraction: 5 = you write one sample and nothing else.
  • Differentiable kernels: 5 = derivatives are built in for every kernel written in the tool.
  • Low-level control: 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched.
  • Works with your arrays: 5 = zero-copy exchange with other frameworks is the norm.
  • Deploy outside Python: 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.
  • Extensibility: 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets.

Uneven ensembles
How long a batch takes when every sample stops at its own step, at the largest batch.
Regular ensembles
How long a batch takes when every sample runs the same number of steps, at the largest batch.
Small jobs
Wall time of the smallest batch, where launch overhead matters most.
Adaptive ODEs
Wall time of an adaptive-step orbit propagator (RK7(8)) at the largest batch.
Memory
Peak memory the process holds for the same workload (device memory on a GPU; host memory on a CPU at N = 1,000,000 only, net of the benchmark harness's own copies).
Compile time
Cold compile of the complex adaptive kernel (RK7(8) orbits) on empty caches; the simple oscillator's time and the growth factor are listed per tool. A tool with nothing to compile sits at the edge. Compiled once per kernel; raptor's compile does not depend on the problem size N.
Code size
Lines of code the task takes, non-blank and non-comment.
Tensor workloads (qualitative)
Tensor workloads (qualitative): how naturally a tool expresses dense array maths (batched linear algebra, convolutions, broadcasting) and how much of it its tuned libraries cover. 5 = this is its home ground.
Array-style programming (qualitative)
Array-style programming (qualitative): how naturally you write whole-array expressions eagerly, the NumPy way. 5 = the array expression is the programming model. Scores are the author's judgement.
Half precision and below (qualitative)
Half precision and below (qualitative): FP16, BF16, FP8 and FP4 arithmetic and tensor cores (FP32 and FP64 are measured on the other axes). 5 = these formats and tensor cores are first-class paths. Scores are the author's judgement.
Single-thread abstraction (qualitative)
Single-thread abstraction (qualitative): how fully you can write the code for one sample, one step, and let the tool run it over the batch: threads, launches, early stopping and scheduling included. 5 = you write one sample and nothing else. Scores are the author's judgement.
Differentiable kernels (qualitative)
Differentiable kernels (qualitative): how directly you get forward- and reverse-mode derivatives of your own kernels, on GPU and on CPU. 5 = built in for every kernel written in the tool's own vocabulary.
Low-level control (qualitative)
Low-level control (qualitative): how much of the GPU's execution you control from the tool's own language: thread indexing, shared memory, atomics, launch shape, synchronisation (raw CUDA/C++ not counted). 5 = you write what each thread does and how it is launched. On a CPU the same question is asked of threads, SIMD and memory layout. Scores are the author's judgement.
Works with your arrays (qualitative)
Works with your arrays (qualitative): how freely arrays move to and from other frameworks without copies. 5 = zero-copy exchange is the norm.
Deploy outside Python (qualitative)
Deploy outside Python (qualitative): whether a compiled kernel can run from programs that are not Python. 5 = a compiled artefact any program can load.
Extensibility (qualitative)
Extensibility (qualitative): how readily new hardware, backends and features can be added without losing speed. 5 = a documented plugin path across many targets. Scores are the author's judgement.

Every measured axis is the per-sample ensemble workload raptor is built for; dense tensor maths, training and half precision are the qualitative axes, where PyTorch and JAX lead. Outer is better; overlaps are complementary, not a ranking.

NVIDIA Warp gives you near-total control of every kernel, short of raw CUDA. raptor hands that control to the engine on purpose, so compaction and the launch shape are decided at run time; the two are different trade-offs, not a ranking.

How to read this radar

Each of the six majors is the plain mean of its minor axes (the detailed radar draws every minor), with equal weights and the same rule for every tool; a minor a tool has no reading on is left out of its mean and the major's marker is drawn hollow. Hover or tap a major to see its minors.

  • Ensemble speed: Uneven ensembles, Regular ensembles, Small jobs and Adaptive ODEs; measured.
  • Footprint and turnaround: Memory, Compile time and Code size; measured.
  • Tensors and precision: Tensor workloads, Array-style programming and Half precision and below; qualitative.
  • One-sample authoring: Single-thread abstraction and Differentiable kernels; qualitative.
  • Low-level control: A single axis, so nothing is averaged; qualitative.
  • Reach: Works with your arrays, Deploy outside Python and Extensibility; qualitative.
